summary: Describes how to take a URI and find an authoritative server for information about it, using the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System. It is part four of the DDDS series and replaces RFCs 2168 and 2915.

plainLanguage.summary: Given a web-style name, DDDS can look up which server is in charge of it. This document says how to do that for URIs.

questions: how to find the authoritative server for a uri
how does ddds resolve a uri
what are the ddds s a u p flags
subtitle: How to turn a URI into a chain of DNS lookups that ends at a server able to answer questions about it.

tldr.problem: URIs and URNs can be brittle over time, and a name that does not say where its resolver lives still needs some way to find an authoritative server for information about it.
tldr.mechanism: This DDDS Application takes the URI scheme (or URN namespace) as a first key under uri.arpa. or urn.arpa., then repeatedly applies rewrite rules stored in NAPTR DNS records until a terminal flag points to a server.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 2168 and RFC 2915 and defines the Application Unique String, flags, service fields and DNS database rules, leaving the actual conversation with the resolver to other specifications.

today: RFC 3404 is a Proposed Standard from October 2002 that obsoletes RFC 2168 and RFC 2915, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It is part four of the DDDS series, so it only makes sense alongside RFC 3401 and the other parts.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
The Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) implements lazy binding of strings to data. It maps a unique string to data in a DDDS Database by repeatedly applying string transformation rules until a terminal condition is reached. This RFC defines only a DDDS Application, the one that resolves Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs). The algorithm and the database are defined elsewhere in the series, which starts with RFC 3401, and the RFC stresses that it is impossible to understand any document in the series without reading the others.

URIs have long been recognized as brittle over time. Uniform Resource Names (URNs) were proposed as persistent, location-independent identifiers, and the Knoxville framework holds that the resolution system must be separate from how names are assigned. That raises one problem: how do you resolve a name that cannot tell you where its resolver is?

For the short term the RFC picks the Domain Name System. It argues DNS is not suitable for per-resource records, since it was never intended to handle that many records, its record size is too limited for catalog information, and domain names are not appropriate as URNs. So DDDS is used to locate resolvers that can provide information about individual resources, rewriting the URI into a Key following the DDDS rules. The document specifies at least one DNS-based Database.
sections.plainLanguage: A name tells you what something is called, not who is in charge of it. This system looks up the person in charge using the phone book, in a few easy steps.

sections.title: URIs Versus URNs
sections.content:
In theory there is no difference between resolving URIs in general and URNs in particular. In practice there is one: if URN resolution were folded into generic URI resolution, URNs could suffer if URI resolution never became widely used.

The solution is a shortcut. Generic URI resolution starts from rules for known URI schemes in the uri.arpa. registry, and the rule for the urn scheme simply delegates to the urn.arpa. zone, which holds NAPTR records by URN namespace. The URI Resolution Rewrite Rule for URN: is thus the URN application's First Well Known Rule. This RFC therefore specifies two DDDS Applications, one for URIs and one for URNs. They are technically identical, but keeping them separate lets URN resolution proceed without the dependency.
sections.plainLanguage: Names of things come in two kinds, and the URN kind has a shortcut straight to its own help desk. That way it still works even if the general help desk is never built.

sections.title: The Application Unique String and First Rule
sections.content:
Every DDDS Application must say what its input string is and how the first key is made. Here the Application Unique String is the URI or URN for which an authoritative server is being located. It MUST be canonicalized and hex encoded according to the absolute-uri production in the Collected ABNF of RFC 2396.

The First Well Known Rule is simple. For a URI, the first key is the URI scheme. For a URN, it is the Namespace Identifier. So http://www.example.com/ has the key http, and urn:foo:foospace has the first key foo.
sections.plainLanguage: The first step is just reading the start of the name, like the 'http' or 'foo' part, and using it to decide where to look next.

sections.title: Flags and Service Fields
sections.content:
Each NAPTR rule carries a flags field and a services field. Four flags are defined: S, A and U are terminal flags that halt the lookup loop, and P hands the rest of the process to application-specific rules outside this document. The four flags are mutually exclusive, and resolution libraries MAY signal an error if more than one is given. Clients MUST NOT assume the flags field holds only 0 or 1 characters, and MUST ignore a record with an unknown flag and move to the next rule. The remaining alphabetic flags are reserved, and numeric flags may be used for local experimentation.

The services field follows an ABNF: an optional protocol followed by zero or more resolution services, each starting with a +. The protocol and each resolution service are limited to 32 characters and must start with a letter. The empty string is valid, which is typical early in a series of rules when it is impossible to know what will be offered at the end of the path. Protocol identifiers MUST be defined by documents specific to URI resolution, and at present THTTP is the only such specification.

Because a client may be satisfied by the first suitable rule and never see a better one, the client may slightly modify the DDDS algorithm for this application to look at further rules while still obeying the Order. This is safe only if the input to step 3 and output of step 4 are identical to the basic algorithm, and the client MUST NOT do this optimization across delegation paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Each pointer comes with a sticky note. One letter says 'this is the final stop, go look up the machine', and another part says what kinds of questions that machine can answer.

sections.title: The DNS Database and uri.arpa.
sections.content:
The only database specified for this Application is the one from RFC 3403, which keeps the rewrite rules in NAPTR DNS resource records. Keys are encoded as domain names. For a URI, the scheme gets .uri.arpa. appended; for a URN, the namespace identifier gets .urn.arpa. appended. That domain is queried for NAPTR records, which produce new keys in the form of domain names.

DNS servers MAY interpret flag values and include appropriate SRV and A records in the Additional Information section of the response. Clients are encouraged, but not required, to check for it. The character set for the substitution expression is UTF-8, the allowed input characters are all those allowed anywhere in a URI, and characters allowed in a Key are those defined for DNS domain names. The i flag on the substitution expression marks a case-insensitive match.

The notes add one rule about ordering: if a record at some order matches the URI but the client does not know the protocol and service, it SHOULD keep examining records with the same order, but MUST NOT consider records with a higher order value. That is what lets site administrators say all requests matching one pattern go to server 1 and all others to server 2.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone book here is DNS. You add 'uri.arpa.' after the first word of the name, look that up, and the answer tells you the next name to look up.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC walks through three cases. In the first, a hypothetical URN urn:foo:002372413:annual-report-1997 gives foo.urn.arpa., which returns three NAPTR records with the s flag at order 100 and preferences 10, 20 and 30, offering foolink, rcds and thttp. A client that knows only RCDS looks up SRV records for rcds.udp.example.com and gets three hosts on port 1000. If SRV and A records come back as additional information along with a long TTL, the average number of DNS probes to resolve most URIs would approach one.

The second case is a made-up cid: URI. Its NAPTR has an empty flags field, so it is not terminal, and uses a regular expression whose substitution extracts the domain example.com for the next lookup. The RFC notes that this example is chosen for teaching and does not conform to the real CID URI scheme. The rule extracts a domain rather than a host name because maintaining records for every machine at a site could be an intolerable burden.

The third resolves http://www.example.com/software/latest-beta.exe. The rule at http.uri.arpa. extracts www.example.com, whose NAPTR records point at mirror services found via SRV records.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like following a treasure map. Each clue gives you the next place to look, and the last clue tells you which house to knock on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using urn.arpa. and uri.arpa. as the registry for namespaces is subject to denial of service attacks and other DNS spoofing attacks. The interaction with DNSSEC was still being studied at the time, and the RFC expects NAPTR records to be signed with SIG records once the DNSSEC work is deployed.

The rewrite rules also make identifiers from other namespaces subject to the same attacks as normal domain names. Regular expressions should be checked for sanity and not blindly passed to something like PERL. Finally, this document only locates a resolver and does not describe communication with it. The security considerations for that communication are outside its scope and must be addressed by the protocols that talk to resolvers.
sections.plainLanguage: Since the system uses the phone book, someone could scribble a wrong number in it. The document says to guard the book and to be careful when following instructions found in it.

items.desc: Terminal. The output is a domain name for which one or more SRV records exist.

items.label: Address lookup
items.desc: Terminal. The output is a domain name to look up A, AAAA or A6 records for.

items.label: URI result
items.desc: Terminal. The output of the rule is a URI.
